title: Twenty First Word First Station Fifth Warning Rejecting Worldly Busyness As An Excuse

questions.question: What main excuse for neglecting worship is challenged at the beginning of this passage?
questions.answer: The excuse that worldly busyness and earning a living leave no time for prayer.

questions.question: According to the passage, how is the human being different from animals in purpose?
questions.answer: Humans are not meant only to chase material needs; they are meant to seek an enduring life in a higher, truly human way.

questions.question: What comparison is used to show human weakness in gaining worldly necessities?
questions.answer: A person is said to be unable to match even a small bird in securing basic worldly provision.

questions.question: What criticism is made of many so-called worldly occupations?
questions.answer: Many of them are described as minor matters that people interfere in without real need.

questions.question: What examples are given of time being wasted on unnecessary knowledge?
questions.answer: The passage mentions spending time on remote facts like details about Saturn’s rings or counting chickens in America.

questions.question: In the example of the worker, what is he invited to do?
questions.answer: He is invited to leave his regular work briefly to dig for a treasure of far greater value.

questions.question: Why is the worker’s refusal presented as foolish?
questions.answer: Because he would give up a huge gain just to avoid a very small loss in wages.

questions.question: In the same way, what happens if a person leaves the required prayers?
questions.answer: The benefit of his labor stays limited to a small, purely worldly income with little true fruit.

questions.question: What is the benefit of using rest times for prayer?
questions.answer: Prayer refreshes the spirit and heart and opens two great sources of benefit for this life and the next.

questions.question: What question is asked to challenge the idea that people are too busy for worship?
questions.answer: The passage asks whether people were created only for worldly life so that all their time should be spent on it.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the real duty of a human being?
questions.answer: To seek a lasting and meaningful life as a human being, not merely to function like an animal.

questions.question: Why is the comparison with animals important in this passage?
questions.answer: It shows that although humans have greater abilities, they are not meant to focus only on feeding and survival.

questions.question: How does the passage describe many of the tasks people call “worldly occupations”?
questions.answer: It says many of them are unimportant matters that people make themselves busy with unnecessarily.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest is wrong with filling life with trivial facts?
questions.answer: It shows a person is acting as if he will remain in this world for an extremely long time.

questions.question: What kind of excuse does the passage answer after discussing unnecessary activities?
questions.answer: It answers the excuse that essential work, especially earning money, keeps a person from prayer.

questions.question: In the example of paid labor, what does the valuable treasure represent?
questions.answer: It represents the immense reward and benefit that come from performing prayer.

questions.question: What does the small wage deduction represent in that example?
questions.answer: It represents the small amount of worldly time or income a person fears losing by stopping for prayer.

questions.question: What lesson is taught by the digging example?
questions.answer: A tiny worldly sacrifice should not make someone miss a far greater and lasting gain.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the result of work without prayer?
questions.answer: Such work remains tied to a narrow worldly return that lacks lasting value.

questions.question: What two kinds of provision are connected to prayer during rest times?
questions.answer: Prayer helps both worldly livelihood in a fruitful way and one’s provision for the hereafter.

questions.question: What is the passage trying to correct in a person’s attitude toward worship?
questions.answer: It is correcting laziness and neglect in worship that are blamed on worldly concerns.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about spending all one’s time on worldly matters?
questions.answer: It implies that doing so forgets the true purpose of being human.

questions.question: Why is the bird comparison humbling?
questions.answer: It reminds people that worldly provision is not where human greatness lies, since even a tiny bird can surpass them in that area.

questions.question: What does the passage say about many topics that occupy people’s minds?
questions.answer: It says they are side issues with little real importance to their main duty.

questions.question: How do the examples of science-like facts function in the argument?
questions.answer: They illustrate how people waste precious time on information that does not truly help their essential purpose.

questions.question: What is the point of the example involving ten minutes of digging?
questions.answer: It shows how irrational it is to reject a massive reward for fear of a very small worldly loss.

questions.question: In the analogy, what does regular daily work stand for in real life?
questions.answer: It stands for one’s effort to earn a living in this world.

questions.question: In the analogy, what stands for the hidden treasure?
questions.answer: It stands for the spiritual and lasting gains linked to the obligatory prayers.

questions.question: According to the passage, what happens to a person’s efforts if prayer is left out?
questions.answer: Their outcome becomes confined to a limited and low-level worldly result.

questions.question: Why are rest periods mentioned specifically?
questions.answer: Because prayer can be placed into those times without destroying one’s work and can even renew the inner self.

questions.question: What inner benefits of prayer are named before the two mines are introduced?
questions.answer: The spirit is rested and the heart is relieved.

questions.question: Which false choice does the passage challenge regarding work and prayer?
questions.answer: It challenges the idea that a person must choose worldly earning instead of worship.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest is mistaken about living as if this world is everything?
questions.answer: It ignores the human calling to prepare for a lasting life beyond this world.

questions.question: How does the passage use the example of animals to teach a lesson about human purpose?
questions.answer: It says humans should not lower themselves to a life centered only on basic survival.

questions.question: What is the problem with becoming absorbed in secondary matters?
questions.answer: A person neglects what is essential while chasing things that do not truly matter.

questions.question: Why are the examples of distant facts intentionally ordinary and even random?
questions.answer: They show how easily people can pour energy into useless information while neglecting worship.

questions.question: What argument does the passage make for people who claim they are busy only with necessary work?
questions.answer: It says even then, leaving prayer for work is unreasonable because prayer brings far greater return than the little time it takes.

questions.question: In the wage example, what does the difference between the small pay and the valuable stones emphasize?
questions.answer: It emphasizes the huge gap between temporary worldly gain and the much greater value of prayer.

questions.question: How does the orchard image connect worldly work and spiritual benefit?
questions.answer: It shows that ordinary labor can become fruitful in both worlds when joined with prayer.

questions.question: What happens to livelihood when prayer is abandoned, according to the passage?
questions.answer: It is reduced to a shallow worldly result lacking higher fruit.

questions.question: How can prayer support even worldly livelihood?
questions.answer: It strengthens the inner self and opens blessed sources of benefit that make one’s worldly work more meaningful and productive.

questions.question: What personal weakness is directly addressed in this warning?
questions.answer: The tendency to become careless in worship because of attachment to worldly life.

questions.question: What assumption about time does the passage question?
questions.answer: It questions the assumption that all one’s available time should go to worldly pursuits.

questions.question: What does the passage teach about human excellence and human limitation?
questions.answer: Humans are higher in capacity and purpose, yet they are not the strongest even in basic worldly provision.

questions.question: Why is comparing a person to a sparrow meaningful here?
questions.answer: It shows that worldly striving alone cannot define human dignity or mission.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about curiosity without purpose?
questions.answer: It can become a trap that consumes time meant for more important responsibilities.

questions.question: How does the passage expose the weakness of the “I’m too busy earning money” excuse?
questions.answer: It shows that even necessary work does not justify missing something far more valuable and brief.

questions.question: In the treasure example, what makes the excuse foolish?
questions.answer: The person refuses an enormous benefit to avoid a tiny reduction in short-term earnings.

questions.question: How is the reader meant to apply that example to real life?
questions.answer: By understanding that stopping for prayer is a small cost compared with its great spiritual reward.

questions.question: What is lacking in livelihood that is cut off from prayer?
questions.answer: It lacks deep value, lasting fruit, and connection to the hereafter.

questions.question: What two immediate inner effects of prayer are mentioned before the mines?
questions.answer: It gives ease to the spirit and relief to the heart.

questions.question: What kind of person is being corrected in this warning?
questions.answer: A person whose love of worldly life makes him lazy and careless about worship.

questions.question: What basic question about creation is raised early in the passage?
questions.answer: Whether a human being was created only for this worldly life.

questions.question: According to the passage, what should a true human being strive for?
questions.answer: A genuine and lasting life beyond the narrow limits of worldly survival.

questions.question: How does the passage use human inability in worldly provision as an argument?
questions.answer: It shows that worldly struggle alone cannot be the main purpose of human existence.

questions.question: What is wrong with interfering in many trivial matters?
questions.answer: It distracts a person from important duties and wastes precious life.

questions.question: What attitude is criticized by the examples about planets and poultry numbers?
questions.answer: Acting like endless time is available and filling it with useless details.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the example of the laborer offered a short extra task?
questions.answer: To show that refusing a very profitable opportunity because of a tiny loss is plainly irrational.

questions.question: What does the orchard represent in the broader teaching of the passage?
questions.answer: It represents one’s place of worldly effort and livelihood.

questions.question: What happens to the “fruits” of one’s work without obligatory prayer?
questions.answer: They remain limited to a weak worldly outcome without lasting spiritual gain.

questions.question: Why does the passage recommend prayer during rest periods?
questions.answer: Because it does not merely take time; it also renews the heart and spirit.

questions.question: What are the two major forms of gain opened by prayer in this section?
questions.answer: Better, more meaningful worldly provision and provision for the hereafter.
